traveler: Nicholas of Cusa (Nikolaus von Kues, Nicolaus Cusanus)
title: The Boatman's Son: Learned Ignorance from the Moselle to Todi
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kues, birth on the Moselle
stops.date_confidence: year attested (1401), day and month unrecorded and defaulted to 01 January. The pin is the corpus's inherited Kues coordinate; note that a verification pass gives the town centroid as 49.91611, 7.06944 and the St. Nikolaus-Hospital as 49.9160, 7.0712, and that the first-pass geographic record placed the birth material at 49.9143, 7.0785, which falls on the Bernkastel bank across the river and is wrong
stops.campa: On the Moselle at Kues, in the Electorate of Trier, a son is born to Johan Krebs, boatman and shipowner, and his wife Katherina Roemer. They call him Nicholas. Johannes Trithemius, born downstream at Trittenheim sixty-one years later, will one day call him in print his countryman from the Moselle, and in 1464 his heart will come back up this same water to be sealed in an altar a few steps from this door. For now the house lives off the river: grain, wine, passengers, and account books that count cargo.
suggested_refs: The birth house at Bernkastel-Kues, still standing and open to visitors
Trithemius, Liber octo quaestionum, written for Emperor Maximilian, which names Cusa as a countryman from the Moselle and quotes the infinite-sphere formula
johannes_trithemius.journey.json
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove; full text not reached)

stops.name: Deventer, the school nobody can document
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and an unresolved one. Meuthen's standard biography flags the Deventer tradition as unproven; the Stanford Encyclopedia does not mention Deventer at all; the Brethren of the Common Life article hedges to 'may have been their pupil'. The conventional c. 1413-14 is carried with month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Older lives put the boy here, in the school the Brethren of the Common Life keep beside the Lebuinuskerk: the devotio moderna, plain Latin, copying as a discipline, the book read slowly and alone. No registry entry has ever been produced for him. The standard modern biography flags the tradition as unproven, one encyclopaedia hedges to may have been their pupil, and a third runs his education straight from the Moselle to Heidelberg without naming the town. What the Brethren taught is not in doubt. Whether he sat in that room is.
suggested_refs: The St. Lebuinus chapter school at Deventer, seat of the Brethren's teaching
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography, on the disputed Deventer tradition
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa' (silent on Deventer)

stops.name: Heidelberg, matriculation in the arts
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1416 by the German matriculation record ('matriculated 1416 in the Artistenfakultaet', as a cleric of the diocese of Trier); the Stanford Encyclopedia gives 1416-17. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Universitaetsplatz: the first-pass record gave 49.3988, 8.6724, a generic centroid about 2.5 km west of the Altstadt
stops.campa: He matriculates in the faculty of arts as a cleric of the diocese of Trier, fifteen years old, at the first of his three universities. There is no Alte Universitat on the square yet; that building goes up between 1712 and 1728. What he walks into is a quarter of rented halls and bursae under the castle hill, where the arts course is read aloud and disputed and a poor clerk pays his way by serving richer ones. He leaves without finishing a degree. In 1417 he crosses the Alps.
suggested_refs: The medieval university quarter of Heidelberg below the castle, not the Alte Universitat building of 1712-1728
The Heidelberg Academy of Sciences edition of the Opera omnia, Felix Meiner, 1932-2006
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Padua, the canon law years
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1417-1423; month and day defaulted. The pin marks the studium quarter, not the Palazzo del Bo, which does not become the university's seat until 1493
stops.campa: Six years at Padua reading canon law. The Palazzo del Bo is not the university's house yet and will not be until 1493; the schools of 1417 are rented rooms along the street the city now calls Via VIII Febbraio. He falls in with men who will run the next thirty years of his life: Giuliano Cesarini, who will one day receive the dedication of his first book, Domenico Capranica, and Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli, physician and mathematician, who measures the sky for a living and talks about it at supper.
suggested_refs: The dispersed schools of the Paduan studium near Via VIII Febbraio, seventy years before the Palazzo del Bo became its seat
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Padua, the doctorate in canon law
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1423; the sources reached give no month or day
stops.campa: He takes the doctorate in canon law at twenty-two. The degree makes him employable in every court of Latin Christendom, because a prince-archbishop, a general council and a pope each need a canonist, and each needs one against the others. He does not stay in Italy. Within two years he is back over the Alps at Cologne, teaching and practising the law he has just been licensed in, while the friends he made in these rooms begin writing to him from the curia.
suggested_refs: The doctoral register of the Paduan faculty of canon law, 1423
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Cologne, the studium and Heimerich de Campo
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: Wikipedia dates the move to Cologne 1425, the Stanford Encyclopedia 1426. Month and day defaulted. The pin is the medieval studium quarter north of the cathedral; the modern University of Cologne, refounded 1919, lies some kilometres southwest and is not this place
stops.campa: He enters Cologne as a doctor of canon law and appears both to teach and to practise there; one source dates the move to 1425 and another to 1426. The medieval studium has no campus: its bursae stand on the Marzellenstrasse just north of the unfinished cathedral, whose crane has stood over the town for a lifetime. Here Heimerich de Campo puts Ramon Llull, Albertus Magnus and Proclus into his hands. He also hunts monastery manuscripts and copies out Plautus comedies that had been given up for lost.
suggested_refs: The bursae of the medieval Cologne studium on the Marzellenstrasse
ramon_llull.journey.json, whose Ars reaches Cusa first through Heimerich de Campo
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Trier, secretary to Otto von Ziegenhain
stops.date_confidence: attested: 'by early February 1425 serving Archbishop Otto von Ziegenhain'. The day within February is not given and is defaulted to 01. A first-pass chronology collapsed this appointment and the 1427 Rome delegation into a single 1427 entry; they are two events in two years and are separated here
stops.campa: By early February he is in the service of Otto von Ziegenhain, Prince-Archbishop of Trier, running a chancery: correspondence, legal briefs, the daily paper of a great see. He learns by hand what a prince-bishopric is. It is a treasury, a court of appeal, a body of vassals who owe service, and a secular neighbour who wants the revenue. Twenty-five years on he will be handed one of his own in the Tirol, with a neighbour of his own. He holds the Trier post until Otto dies in 1430.
suggested_refs: The archiepiscopal chancery of Trier under Otto von Ziegenhain, 1425-1430
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Rome, the first legation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1427 ('Rome journey: 1427, first papal visit, on Otto's orders'); month and day not given in the sources reached
stops.campa: His archbishop sends him south as episcopal delegate, and he sees the curia for the first time: Old St. Peter's, still the basilica Constantine raised, the papacy barely a decade home from Avignon and its authority contested by half of Christendom. He comes as a junior canonist carrying somebody else's brief. He will be back as a cardinal, and again as vicar general of the Papal States. What the errand of 1427 actually was, no source reached will say.
suggested_refs: Old St. Peter's Basilica, the Constantinian church still standing in 1427
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Koblenz, the deanery of St. Florin
stops.date_confidence: attested: the benefice list gives the deanery of St. Florin at Koblenz as held 1427-1445. Month and day defaulted. An English account dating the appointment to 1430 is impossible, since Otto von Ziegenhain, who conferred it, died that year
stops.campa: Otto sets him up with benefices. Chief among them is the deanery of St. Florin at Koblenz, a collegiate church standing where the Moselle runs into the Rhine. The deanery is an income and not a residence: he draws it while living mostly elsewhere, which is how a churchman without land of his own is paid in the fifteenth century, and how a boatman's son acquires the means to go wherever the law takes him. He holds it from 1427 to 1445, eighteen years.
suggested_refs: The Florinskirche at Koblenz, collegiate church of his longest-held benefice

stops.name: Paris, reading Ramon Llull
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1428; month and day not given. The pin follows the university-quarter coordinate already carried in this journey rather than the corpus civic pin for Paris, a deliberate deviation and not a slip. A verification pass gives the Sorbonne building itself as 48.8485, 2.3432; the first-pass geographic record gave 48.8534, 2.3488, which lands on the Right Bank outside the quarter entirely
stops.campa: He goes to Paris at his own expense to read Ramon Llull in manuscript, copying out of the great combinatory system whatever he can use: the wheels of terms, the art of turning a figure until everything that may truly be said of God has been said. Nobody sends him. Llull is the one master he goes looking for. The quires he copies here travel home with him to the Moselle, and they sit in the library at Kues today. Louvain offers him a chair this same year, and offers again in 1435, and he refuses both times.
suggested_refs: The Llull manuscripts copied by Cusa in Paris, still in his own library at Kues
ramon_llull.journey.json, which carries no reciprocal reference to Cusa and should
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Nuremberg, the diet and the Manderscheid brief
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1431; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Otto died in 1430 and the see fell into a contested election, chapter against pope. At the imperial diet Nicholas appears as advocate for Ulrich von Manderscheid, whom the Trier chapter has elected and the pope refuses to confirm. It is a lawyer's brief, taken for a client and paid for by him, and it puts him before the assembled princes on a question the diet has no machinery to settle. Who makes a bishop: the chapter that elects him, the pope who confirms him, or a council sitting above them both?
suggested_refs: The imperial diet of Nuremberg, 1431, and the disputed Trier succession
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

segments.name: Basel: the Council and the Forgery

stops.name: Basel, arriving at the council
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1432; month and day defaulted. The pin is the Basel Munster, where the council sat
stops.campa: He arrives at the Council of Basel for his client and stays five years for the argument. The council is sitting in defiance of a pope who has tried to dissolve it, and it votes by heads rather than by nations, so that a doctor of canon law counts for as much in the hall as an archbishop. Its central claim, that a general council represents the whole Church and outranks the man in Rome, he takes up with both hands. Within a year of arriving he is writing the constitutional case for it at book length.
suggested_refs: The Basel Munster, seat of the council from 1431
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Basel, the Donation of Constantine unmasked
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: the Stanford Encyclopedia dates De concordantia catholica to 1433, Wikipedia gives no year at all and says only that he wrote it while at the council, and the Wikiquote attribution to the translated text carries 1434. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He writes De concordantia catholica inside the council's own house: a constitution for Christendom in which authority rises from consent, councils bind popes, and even the election of the King of the Romans is reformed so that each elector ranks every candidate in order rather than naming one. Sifting the documents that underwrite papal temporal power, he sets the Latin of the Donation of Constantine against the Latin of the fourth century and declares it a forgery. He is thirty-two.
stops.quote: All men are free by nature
stops.quote_source: De Concordantia Catholica (1433/34); trans. Kevin Gallagher
suggested_refs: De concordantia catholica, book III, on the reform of the imperial election, an early precursor of the Borda count
Lorenzo Valla, De falso credita et ementita Constantini donatione, an independent demonstration of the same forgery some years later
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Basel, crossing to the pope
stops.date_confidence: attested: his departure from Basel is dated 17 May 1437
stops.campa: Five years in, the council splits over where to meet the Greeks, and he crosses. The majority votes for Basel or Avignon; the minority votes for an Italian city, which is the only thing Constantinople will accept, and Nicholas signs with the minority and with Eugenius IV. The conciliarist of De concordantia catholica becomes the pope's man in the space of one decree. He rides out on 17 May with a papal commission in his baggage. His old colleagues never let the reversal go, and why he made it the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The divided decree of the Council of Basel on the site of the union council, 1437
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

segments.name: The Greek Embassy and the Illumination

stops.name: Venice, taking ship for the Bosporus
stops.date_confidence: the embarkation is placed in May-June 1437; the day is not given and is defaulted. The Venice pin is the corpus coordinate, inherited unchanged
stops.campa: He rides out of Basel on 17 May and takes ship at Venice with the papal delegation. The commission is to bring back an emperor: John VIII Palaiologos, his patriarch, and enough Greek bishops to make the union of the churches look like a council rather than a surrender. Whichever delegation returns with the emperor wins the argument over who speaks for the Church. Behind them the rump at Basel is fitting out a rival embassy on the same errand, so that two Latin fleets sail east that summer for the same Greeks.
suggested_refs: The Molo at Venice, embarkation point of the papal embassy of 1437

stops.name: Constantinople, the delegation lands
stops.date_confidence: the arrival on 24 September 1437 is attested, as is the westward departure in November. The Hagia Sophia coordinate is scene-setting: no source reached places his negotiations inside that church, and no source reached names the site of any imperial audience, so no audience stop is staged here
stops.campa: The delegation reaches Constantinople on 24 September, and the negotiation runs through the autumn: which city, at whose expense, on what agenda, and whether the emperor of the Romans can leave his capital at all with the Turks at the throat of it. He is in the city sixteen years before its walls are broken. What he carries home is not only the Greek party but Greek manuscripts and the habit of arguing with theologians who concede nothing whatever to the Latin vocabulary. In November the ships turn west.
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia, the great church of the Wisdom of God, standing sixteen years before the conquest
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: The Aegean, the illumination at sea
stops.date_confidence: the illumination is attested only in his own dedicatory letter to Cesarini, which gives neither date nor position, saying only that it came at sea returning from Greece. The fleet sailed west from Constantinople in November 1437 and landed at Venice on 8 February 1438, so December 1437 is a placement within an attested window; the coordinate is a symbolic midpoint on that route. A first-pass record dated this 'autumn 1438', which is a year out
stops.campa: Somewhere on the water between Greece and Italy, on the return crossing, it comes to him. He describes it years afterward in the dedicatory letter to Cardinal Cesarini as a thing received from the Father of lights rather than worked out: that the infinite cannot be reached by any proportion of finite things, and that the whole human approach to it is a learned ignorance, a knowing of the not-knowing. The ship under him is carrying an emperor and a patriarch west to a council. He gives it no date and no position.
stops.quote: there is no proportion between finite and infinite
stops.quote_source: De Docta Ignorantia, Book I; trans. Jasper Hopkins
suggested_refs: The dedicatory letter to Giuliano Cesarini appended to De docta ignorantia, his only account of the shipboard illumination
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Venice, the return landing
stops.date_confidence: attested: the return landing at Venice is dated 8 February 1438, and the Byzantine contingent reaches Ferrara in early April 1438
stops.campa: The fleet lands at Venice on 8 February with the Greek party aboard: the emperor, the Patriarch Joseph II, and the bishops. The embassy has done what it was sent to do, in nine months, and it has beaten the Basel ships to the harbour. His part was the fetching; what follows is not his to negotiate. The Greeks reach Ferrara in early April, and the union will be argued there and at Florence, signed in 1439, and repudiated in Constantinople almost as soon as they are home again.
suggested_refs: The arrival of John VIII Palaiologos and Patriarch Joseph II at Venice, February 1438
The Council of Ferrara-Florence, opened for the Greeks in April 1438

segments.name: The Papal Cause in the German Lands

stops.name: Kues, finishing De docta ignorantia
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested by the colophon: he finished the book on 12 February 1440. The place is not attested anywhere reached. The sources say only that he was in Germany rather than at sea; this pin defaults to the Moselle, while a first-pass geographic record proposed Koblenz on the strength of the St. Florin provostship. Both are reconstructions and the disagreement is left standing
stops.campa: He finishes De docta ignorantia on 12 February 1440, two years after the crossing that gave it to him, and sends it to Cesarini with the account of how it came. In it the universe has no fixed centre and no circumference, the earth is not at rest and is a star among stars, and maximum and minimum coincide where the finite gives out. The argument is not astronomy. It descends from the doctrine that God is everywhere and nowhere, which leaves no point outside the world from which a centre could be fixed.
stops.quote: The world-machine will have its center everywhere and its circumference nowhere, so to speak; for God, who is everywhere and nowhere, is its circumference and center.
stops.quote_source: De Docta Ignorantia, Book II, ch. 12 (162:15-17); trans. Jasper Hopkins, Nicholas of Cusa on Learned Ignorance (Banning Press, 2nd ed.)
suggested_refs: De docta ignorantia, Book II, on a universe with no centre and no circumference
giordano_bruno.journey.json, for the cosmology a later Nolan will restate as a physical infinity rather than a theological one
Alexandre Koyre, From the Closed World to the Infinite Universe (1957), which traces the descent
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Mainz, the diet and the conjectures
stops.date_confidence: the Mainz diet is attested for 1441; month and day defaulted. De coniecturis is dated 1441-42 by Wikipedia and 1442-43 by the Stanford Encyclopedia, and the disagreement is not resolved. The 1444 purchases fall three years after the stop's stamped date and are placed in this campa because their location is nowhere recorded
stops.campa: Another diet, another season of putting the papal case to German princes who have declared neutrality between pope and council and mean to keep it. In these years between the road and the chancery he writes De coniecturis, which holds that every positive human assertion of truth is a conjecture, a participation in truth but in otherness. In 1444 he buys sixteen books on astronomy, a wooden celestial globe, a copper one, and instruments including an astrolabe. Where he buys them is not recorded.
stops.quote: every positive human assertion of the truth is a conjecture
stops.quote_source: De Coniecturis (On Conjectures), Prologue; trans. Jasper Hopkins
suggested_refs: De coniecturis, on conjecture as the whole reach of human assertion
The surviving instrument collection of the Cusanusstift, 13th to 15th century
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Romer and the Hercules of the Eugenians
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1446 Frankfurt Reichstag legation; month and day defaulted. The epithet is Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini's, recorded in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia; a first-pass record attached it to a Mainz scene of 1447 that does not stand
stops.campa: At the Reichstag he works the princes and electors for the papacy, one legate among several trying to end the Empire's long neutrality in the standoff between Eugenius IV and the rump still sitting at Basel. The negotiations are procedural and slow, conducted across the Romer's council chambers over sessions that run for years. Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini, on the other side of some of these rooms and one day pope himself, calls him the Hercules of the Eugenians.
suggested_refs: The Romer at Frankfurt, chamber of the 1446 Reichstag negotiations
Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini's epithet, recorded in the Catholic Encyclopedia of 1913
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Aschaffenburg, the princes decide
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Princes' Concordat is concluded in January 1447 and the German chronology lists Aschaffenburg 1447. Day defaulted. A first-pass record staged this scene at Mainz and credited Cusa with the Concordat of Vienna of 1448, which was signed for the papacy by Cardinal Juan Carvajal and does not name him; his documented Mainz diet is 1441
stops.campa: In January the German electors finally decide for the pope, and fifteen years of imperial neutrality end. He has spent the better part of two decades on the single question of who may bind the Church, arguing one answer at Basel and the opposite answer everywhere since. Nothing he signs here belongs to the Concordat of Vienna the following year, which is Cardinal Juan Carvajal's work. The castle the princes meet in is the medieval Johannisburg; it burns in 1552, and the palace that now carries the name is not begun until 1605.
suggested_refs: The princes' assembly at Aschaffenburg, January 1447
The medieval Johannisburg castle, burned 1552, not the Renaissance palace begun 1605

stops.name: Rome, named cardinal in his absence
stops.date_confidence: attested: created cardinal in pectore by Nicholas V on 20 December 1448, published January 1449. Eugenius IV had nominated or intended him in 1446 but died on 23 February 1447 without publishing, so the German chronology records only 'planned by Eugen IV before his death'. A first-pass chronology treated the 1446 nomination as a creation; the two acts are separated here
stops.campa: Nicholas V creates him cardinal in pectore on 20 December, and the name is published in January. Eugenius IV had intended the same honour two years earlier and died before publishing it, so the record carries two nominations and one cardinal. He is in Germany when it happens, on the road as usual, and he does not come south for the hat until the jubilee year. The boatman's son from the Moselle is forty-seven years old and has never held a bishopric.
suggested_refs: The consistory of 20 December 1448 and the publication of January 1449
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, the red hat and the title
stops.date_confidence: attested: red hat received 11 January 1450 at Rome, with the title of San Pietro in Vincoli; the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia dates the proclamation as cardinal-priest of St Peter ad Vincula to 1449. Coordinate corrected from 41.8955, 12.4917, which sits about 220 m northwest of the basilica
stops.campa: He comes to Rome in the jubilee year and receives the hat on 11 January, with the title of San Pietro in Vincoli on the Esquiline, the basilica raised to hold the chains that bound Peter at Jerusalem and at Rome, joined by legend into one relic. He signs the name of this church beneath his own from now on, and he will be buried in it. In the same jubilee crowds he sets the Idiota dialogues, in which a layman who carves wooden spoons instructs an orator and a philosopher on the mind.
stops.quote: Mind [mens] takes its name from measuring [mensurare].
stops.quote_source: Idiota de Mente (The Layman on Mind), I.57; trans. Jasper Hopkins, Nicholas of Cusa on Wisdom and Knowledge (Banning Press, 1996), p. 533
suggested_refs: San Pietro in Vincoli, his titular church from 1449 and his grave from 1464
Idiota de sapientia, de mente and de staticis experimentis, all of 1450, set among the jubilee crowds
sources: Jasper Hopkins, Nicholas of Cusa on Wisdom and Knowledge (1996)

stops.name: Brixen, consecrated bishop
stops.date_confidence: attested: appointed bishop of Brixen 23 March 1450, consecrated 26 April 1450, commissioned papal legate to the German lands 24 December 1450. One English account calls the April rite an ordination, which it is not; he had been a priest since some year in the 1430s that no source reached fixes
stops.campa: Appointed on 23 March and consecrated on 26 April, he receives a diocese in the Tirol whose secular overlord, Duke Sigismund of Austria, considers the naming of its bishop his own business. Brixen is a small Alpine see on the road over the Brenner, rich in tolls and poor in castles the bishop actually holds. He does not go there. On 24 December he is commissioned papal legate to the German lands instead, and the diocese waits two years for its bishop while its bishop rides.
suggested_refs: Brixen Cathedral, seat of the diocese he was consecrated to and could not hold
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Salzburg, the legation begins
stops.date_confidence: weak. The legation itself is attested from its commission of 24 December 1450 to early spring 1452, and its scale of nearly three thousand miles is attested; the city-by-city itinerary is not. The German chronology gives no route at all, and Salzburg rests on Meuthen alone, not reached directly in this session. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Great Legation begins: nearly three thousand miles through the German lands with a mandate to preach the jubilee indulgence, hold reform synods, visit monasteries and put clerical discipline back on its feet. Salzburg is among the archiepiscopal seats where he holds a synod and preaches. He carries a standard set of instructions, corrected liturgical calendars and injunctions against simony and lax observance, applied diocese by diocese with little patience for local custom. Some houses comply. Others wait him out.
suggested_refs: The provincial synods of the Great Legation, 1451-1452
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove; the itinerary rests on this source alone)

stops.name: Vienna, preaching in the Stephansdom
stops.date_confidence: the Vienna leg is named for 1451 but not dated; as with the rest of the legation itinerary it rests on Meuthen, not reached directly. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: At Vienna he preaches beneath the unfinished tower and does reform business with the Austrian clergy and with a university faculty that has its own inertia and no wish to be corrected by a cardinal passing through. He inspects the chapter's discipline, orders corrections to concubinage and absentee benefices, and preaches the jubilee to whoever comes. The faculty complies on paper. He is in the city a matter of days, and then the legation moves on north.
suggested_refs: St. Stephen's Cathedral, Vienna, a legation preaching station of 1451
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Magdeburg, the northern limit
stops.date_confidence: the Magdeburg leg could not be confirmed city by city: the German chronology gives only the commission date and the spring 1452 end, so this rests on Meuthen alone. Month and day defaulted. Coordinate corrected from 52.1259, 11.6389, which sat about 335 m northeast of the cathedral toward the Elbe
stops.campa: The legation reaches Magdeburg, one of its farthest points north and well past the Alpine dioceses he knows. He addresses the cathedral chapter on discipline and on its finances. A local pilgrimage cult also draws his notice: relics pulling crowds on evidence he judges thin. He does not shut it down. He tightens the rules instead, requiring better documentation before a shrine may claim miraculous power, and leaves the cult standing under a stricter test of its papers than it had before he came.
suggested_refs: Magdeburg Cathedral, station of the legation's northern reach
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove; unconfirmed leg)

stops.name: Utrecht, the far edge of the circuit
stops.date_confidence: the Low Countries leg is dated 1452 by the first-pass geographic record, which also dated Wurzburg 1451 while calling Liege and Utrecht the final northern stretch, an internal ordering inconsistency it flagged and did not fix. Month and day defaulted; the leg rests on Meuthen alone
stops.campa: Utrecht is close to the furthest the legation reaches into the Low Countries before the long circuit turns back toward home ground. Something near three thousand miles in under two years, diocese after diocese, correcting calendars and rooting out the same small abuses at every stop. What it leaves behind is a trail of tightened statutes across half the Empire and no single victory anyone can point at. In the spring of 1452 the commission ends and he turns south for the Tirol, fifty-one years old, to take up a diocese he has never governed.
suggested_refs: The Dom of Utrecht, near the outer limit of the Great Legation
sources: Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove; unconfirmed leg)

stops.name: Brixen, taking up the diocese
stops.date_confidence: attested: the legation ends in early spring 1452 and active administration of Brixen begins that year, with resistance from Sigismund immediate. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In the spring the legation ends and he goes at last to govern Brixen. Sigismund has been waiting. The duke holds the advocacy of the diocese, its castles and the loyalty of its nobles; the bishop holds the law and the pope, and has spent his life arguing that jurisdiction is settled by right reason and consent. The first year goes on who confirms appointments, who takes the revenues, and whose men garrison the valleys. At Sonnenburg in the Pustertal the Benedictine nuns refuse his visitation, and go on refusing until the thing stands near an armed standoff.
suggested_refs: The Brixen jurisdictional conflict of 1452-1460 between bishop and Duke Sigismund
The Benedictine convent of Sonnenburg in the Pustertal, which refused his reform
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Erich Meuthen, Nicholas of Cusa: A Sketch for a Biography (at one remove)

stops.name: Brixen, the year Constantinople falls
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1453: both De visione Dei, written at the request of the monks of Tegernsee, and De pace fidei, written in the wake of the fall of Constantinople in May, are dated to this year. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Constantinople falls in May, and the news reaches him in the Tirol sixteen years after he sailed into that harbour to fetch its emperor west. He answers with two books in one year. De visione Dei, written for the monks of Tegernsee, turns on an icon whose eyes meet each man wherever he stands, and reasons from that painted gaze to a wall of paradise inside which seeing and being seen are one act. De pace fidei seats the wise of every nation before the throne of heaven.
stops.quote: O Lord, when you look upon me with an eye of graciousness, what is your seeing, other than your being seen by me?
stops.quote_source: De Visione Dei, ch. 5 (1453); trans. Jasper Hopkins
suggested_refs: De visione Dei, sent to Tegernsee with an all-seeing icon as its demonstration
The wall of paradise, the boundary within which opposites coincide
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Temple Mount, the council in heaven
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Cusa never travelled to Jerusalem. The canonical corpus pin is inherited unchanged to mark the traditions his 1453 dialogue seats at its council, a conceptual and not a physical stop
stops.campa: He never goes to Jerusalem. The traditions his 1453 dialogue seats at its council are rooted at this rock, which all three of the peoples of the book count holy, and he writes about them from a valley in the Tirol in the year the Turks take Constantinople. In the dialogue the Word summons a spokesman from every nation before the throne, and the Jew, the Christian, the Arab, the Persian and the Indian are brought to see that their difference is one of usage and not of God.
stops.quote: You know, Lord, that a great multitude cannot exist without much diversity
stops.quote_source: De Pace Fidei (1453); trans. William F. Wertz
suggested_refs: De pace fidei, the heavenly council of one religion in a variety of rites

stops.name: Andraz, the bishop in the mountain keep
stops.date_confidence: attested: the refuge at Andraz (Buchenstein) runs from July 1457 to September 1458; the day within July is not given and is defaulted
stops.campa: The feud goes to ground. Threatened in his own cathedral city, he withdraws in July to the castle of Andraz, high in the Dolomite valleys, and stays fourteen months with the duke's men in the valley below and his own church out of reach. Sigismund's case is that the advocacy of Brixen belongs to him, and that a bishop out of the Moselle is a foreigner in the Tirol. Cusa's case is canon law. On 5 April 1458 the two sides meet in arms at Enneberg in the Gadertal. He comes down from the keep in September.
stops.quote: Wisdom is not to be found in the art of oratory, or in great books, but in a withdrawal from these sensible things and in a turning to the most simple and infinite forms.
stops.quote_source: De Docta Ignorantia (1440); trans. John Patrick Dolan (1962)
suggested_refs: Buchenstein (Andraz) castle, his refuge from July 1457 to September 1458
The armed clash at Enneberg in the Gadertal, 5 April 1458, between the bishop's men and the duke's

stops.name: Kues, the hospital on the family ground
stops.date_confidence: attested: the founding deed of the St. Nikolaus-Hospital is dated 3 December 1458, with the buildings erected from 1451 to 1456. A first-pass record dated the foundation itself 1451, conflating charter with building campaign, and this file's own lenses contradicted each other on the point. Coordinate 49.9160, 7.0712 per the hospital's own record, not the 49.9143, 7.0785 of the first pass, which falls across the river
stops.campa: By deed of 3 December he and his siblings endow a hospice on the Moselle bank where the boats used to load: thirty-three places for the years of Christ's life, six for nobles, six for priests, twenty-one for common men, with a chapel and a library. The building has been going up since 1451. To it he leaves his whole inheritance and his books, the Cologne manuscripts, the Llull he copied at Paris, the sixteen astronomy volumes and the two celestial globes. The same instrument gives directions for the burial of his heart in the chapel.
suggested_refs: The St. Nikolaus-Hospital (Cusanusstift) at Bernkastel-Kues, founded by deed of 3 December 1458 and still a home for the aged
The Cusanusstift library, among the most important surviving private libraries of the Middle Ages

stops.name: Rome, vicar general of the Papal States
stops.date_confidence: attested: summoned to Rome by the newly elected Pius II on 30 September 1458, made legate and vicar general in the Papal States on 11 January 1459. A first-pass geographic record dated this appointment 1461 and his departure from the Tyrol 1461; both are wrong, and the departure is 27 April 1460
stops.campa: Pius II, elected in August, called him back to Rome on 30 September, and on 11 January he is made legate and vicar general of the Papal States, governing Rome and its territory whenever the pope travels. The two have known each other since Basel, when the new pope was Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini and both of them served a council they later abandoned. He writes De beryllo in this period, on the small beryl lens that lets an eye take in what is otherwise too fine or too far to be seen at all.
suggested_refs: De beryllo, 1458, on the lens as an image of intellectual sight
The commission as legate and vicar general in the Papal States, 11 January 1459
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Bruneck, the siege and the capitulation
stops.date_confidence: attested: the siege runs from Easter 1460 and the capitulation is dated 17 April 1460
stops.campa: Sigismund brings up one of the heaviest bombards yet used in the field and lays siege to the bishop's residence at Bruneck over Easter. On 17 April Nicholas capitulates and signs what is put in front of him. He is fifty-nine, taken in his own castle by the advocate of his own diocese, and the terms are dictated. Pius II will excommunicate the duke for it and lay the whole Tirol under interdict, and none of that gives the bishop his church back. He does not see Brixen again.
suggested_refs: Bruneck castle, besieged at Easter 1460, and the great bombard brought against it

stops.name: Siena, carrying the defeat to the pope
stops.date_confidence: attested: he leaves the Tyrol for Siena from 27 April 1460 onward and never returns to Brixen
stops.campa: Ten days after the surrender he leaves the Tyrol for good and carries the humiliation south in person: a cardinal of the Roman Church driven out of his see by a duke, arriving at the Sienese court of Pius II to ask what the Church intends to do about it. Pius excommunicates Sigismund and lays the whole Tirol under interdict. In the mountains both are ignored. He does not cross the Brenner again, and everything he writes from here on is written in Italy, by a bishop who governs his diocese on paper.
suggested_refs: The court of Pius II at Siena, spring 1460

segments.name: The Roman Exile and the Last Books

stops.name: Rome, sifting the Qur'an
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1461 by the Stanford Encyclopedia, which dates both Cribratio Alchorani and De li non aliud to that year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Settled in Rome as an exile from his own bishopric, sixty years old and holding a diocese he cannot enter, he goes back to the desk. Cribratio Alchorani sifts the Qur'an sura by sura, weighing what a Christian may accept in it, eight years after the fall of Constantinople and in a curia that talks of little but crusade. In the same season he writes De li non aliud, in which God is named the Not-Other: not one more thing standing beside things, but that by which each thing is itself and not another.
stops.quote: Not Other is not an other, nor is it other than any other
stops.quote_source: De Li Non Aliud (On the Not-Other), ch. 6 (1461); trans. Jasper Hopkins
suggested_refs: Cribratio Alchorani, 1461, a sifting of the Qur'an sura by sura
De li non aliud, on God as the Not-Other
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Mecca, the house he argues with and never sees
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Cusa never travelled to Arabia. The canonical corpus pin is inherited byte-identical to mark the subject of the Cribratio, a conceptual and not a physical stop
stops.campa: He never travels to Arabia. The sifting is done at a Roman desk, out of a Latin Qur'an and a polemical tradition that has spent four centuries calling the Prophet an impostor. He does not use that tradition the way it was built to be used. He treats the men he is disputing with as people who might be persuaded, weighs the book for what a Christian can accept in it, and argues that where it is read rightly the gospel is already present in it. Mecca he knows as a name inside the text.
suggested_refs: The Latin Qur'an tradition available in Rome in 1461, the text underlying the Cribratio
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Rome, the ball that will not run straight
stops.date_confidence: attested: De venatione sapientiae 1462, De ludo globi 1462-63. Month and day defaulted; the two works are carried in one stop
stops.campa: De venatione sapientiae surveys every field in which he has hunted wisdom and counts the game taken. Then De ludo globi, built around a game he plays with visitors: a wooden ball hollowed on one side so that its weight sits off centre, so that however it is thrown it wobbles and curves and comes to rest along a spiral nobody can predict. He reads the soul into that path, restless, never moving straight, drawn at last toward its own centre. The ball is on the floor of a room in Rome and the argument is about God.
stops.quote: A conjecture, then, is a positive assertion that participates in truth as it is, but in otherness
stops.quote_source: De Coniecturis (On Conjectures), Book I, ch. 11; trans. Jasper Hopkins
suggested_refs: De ludo globi, the bowling game with an off-centre ball
gottfried_wilhelm_leibniz.journey.json, for a later claim that the coincidence of opposites stands among the ancestors of his thought, currently attested nowhere but in this file
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: Rome, the city with five gates
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left standing: the German chronology dates the Compendium 1463/64, the Stanford Encyclopedia and MacTutor both 1464, and this file's own first-pass lenses split between the two. Month and day defaulted. The chapter number (cap. viii) is secondary-literature consensus and matches the Latin as printed by Harper's, but the critical edition (Opera Omnia XI/3) was not reachable and jasper-hopkins.info is offline, so Hopkins' section and page numbering is unverified
stops.campa: In the Compendium he sets the mind inside a walled city. Five gates open in the wall, one for each sense, and through them messengers come in continually with news of the world outside: light and colour by the gate of sight, sound and voice by hearing, then odours, then flavours, then heat and cold each by their own. At the centre sits a cosmographer who never leaves the city and never sees a coast, and out of the dispatches alone he draws one map. Then he dismisses the messengers, shuts the gates, and turns to look at the maker.
stops.quote: a completely developed animal in which there is both sense and intellect is to be likened to a geographer who dwells in a city that has the five gateways of the five senses
stops.quote_source: Compendium, ch. 8 (1464); trans. Jasper Hopkins, Nicholas of Cusa on Wisdom and Knowledge (Banning Press, 1996), which renders cosmographus as geographer
suggested_refs: Compendium cap. viii, the civitas mentis and the cosmographer's map
Scott Horton, 'Nicholas of Kues: the Cosmographer's Tale', Harper's Magazine, No Comment, 18 November 2007, which prints the Latin
The History of Cartography, vol. 3 pt. 1, ch. 25, ed. Harley and Woodward, on the passage as cartographic epistemology

Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicholas of Cusa'
Harper's Magazine, Scott Horton, 18 November 2007 (Latin text)
Jasper Hopkins, Nicholas of Cusa on Wisdom and Knowledge (1996)

stops.name: Todi, the road to Ancona ends
stops.date_confidence: attested: 11 August 1464 at Todi in Umbria, travelling from Rome toward Ancona. Pius II died at Ancona on 14 August, three days later, not eleven as a first-pass record had it. MacTutor reports Toscanelli present at the death; no second source reached confirms it. The June 1464 settlement is given by the German chronology, while the English article says only that Sigismund surrendered after Cusa's death, with no interval
stops.campa: Pius II has proclaimed a crusade and gone to Ancona to sail with it. Nicholas, sixty-three and ill, travels south-east from Rome to join him and gets as far as Todi on its hill above the Tiber valley, where he dies on 11 August. Pius dies at Ancona on the fourteenth, having watched the Venetian galleys come in from a window two days earlier, too late to board. The Brixen quarrel had been settled in June on terms leaving Cusa bishop in name while another man exercised the office.
stops.quote: I see, Lord, through Thine infinite mercy, that Thou art Infinity encompassing all things.
stops.quote_source: De Visione Dei (1453); trans. Emma Gurney Salter (1960 reprint)
suggested_refs: Todi, Umbria, where he died on 11 August 1464
De apice theoriae, his last short treatise, written in the year of his death
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Nicholas of Cusa'

stops.name: San Pietro in Vincoli, the grave that was lost
stops.date_confidence: the interment in his titular church is attested and the exact original grave spot is reported lost; no source reached gives a date for either the burial or the loss, so the stop carries the death date. Coordinate corrected from 41.8955, 12.4917, about 220 m northwest of the basilica
stops.campa: His body is carried to Rome and buried in his titular church, probably near the relic of Peter's chains. He has held the title since the jubilee of 1450. The grave itself was afterwards lost. When it was lost, or how, or whether anyone at the time thought the loss worth recording, no source consulted will say. What stands above ground is two tombstones, one medieval and one modern, and Andrea Bregno's relief of a cardinal kneeling before Saint Peter. The chains are in the confessio beneath the high altar.
suggested_refs: Andrea Bregno's relief, Cardinal Nicholas before St Peter, San Pietro in Vincoli
The two further tombstones, medieval and modern, in the same church

stops.name: Kues, the heart in the chapel altar
stops.date_confidence: the heart burial at the Cusanusstift is attested in both language editions; no source reached gives a date for the deposition, so the stop carries the death date. The lunar crater Cusanus is on the near side at 72.0 N 70.8 E, 60.9 km across, not on the far side as a first-pass record had it
stops.campa: His heart goes home. By his own bequest it is taken out, carried up the Moselle and sealed in the chapel altar of the hospice at Kues, a few steps from the house where the boatman's son was born. A crater sixty-one kilometres across on the north-eastern limb of the Moon carries his name; from Earth it is always seen at an angle. The hospice still takes in the aged. The library he stocked for it still holds the manuscripts he bought at Cologne and the Llull he copied at Paris.
suggested_refs: The chapel altar of the St. Nikolaus-Hospital at Bernkastel-Kues, holding his heart
The lunar crater Cusanus, 72.0 N 70.8 E, 60.9 km across, foreshortened from Earth by its position on the limb
The Nicolai de Cusa Opera Omnia of the Heidelberg Academy, Felix Meiner, 1932-2006
